An OpenComputer is a machine you control that you have connected to MIOSA through OpenComputers: a server, workstation, GPU box, or existing hosted server.

It can run anywhere. The connection model does not define its physical location.

In MIOSA, your lab server, once registered, appears as an OpenComputer you can run commands on. It is different from BYOC worker capacity.

Related: OpenComputers, Computer, MIOSA-managed Computer, Host key, Host fingerprint, On-premises server, Tunnel

### OpenComputers

OpenComputers is the system for connecting machines you already own to MIOSA and operating them remotely: commands, containers, tunnels, CI runners, backups, and agent work.

Use it when work must run on hardware you control. You install a host agent, it opens an outbound connection, and MIOSA manages the machine as a host.

In MIOSA, connecting a machine does not install the full MIOSA control plane on it. You keep the hardware, OS, and the decision about what the agent may reach.

Related: OpenComputer, On-premises server, Host key, Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC), Data residency

### Placement

Placement is the decision of where an eligible workload will run: which host or pool among those allowed.

It follows policy and capability, such as region, size, and whether a host supports what you need. You normally do not choose a host directly.

In MIOSA, the scheduler matches a workload's CPU, RAM, and region needs against the free capacity of the fleet. In hybrid setups, policy can keep governed workloads on your own infrastructure.

Related: Worker pool, Hybrid infrastructure, Capability, Control plane

### Region

A Region is the place where a Sandbox or Computer runs. Each resource is created in exactly one region and stays there for its lifetime.

Pick by data rules first, then by closeness to your users or CI so connections are quicker. The three US regions perform about the same for most people.

In MIOSA, regions are `us-west` (Los Angeles, the default), `us-east` (New York), and `us-mia` (Miami). `miosa regions` shows what is available and whether there is capacity.

Related: Placement, Data residency, Sandbox, Computer, Customer-cloud region

### Replica

A Replica is one of several identical copies of a dynamic app running at the same time. More replicas handle more visitors and keep the app up if one fails.

By default a dynamic service has one. Raise it when you need more capacity or resilience.

In MIOSA, you set `desired_replicas`, and the reconciler spreads copies across hosts, and across zones where possible. Traffic is shared among healthy replicas.

Related: Runtime Instance, Dynamic deployment, Reconciliation

### runtime_profile (sandbox field)

A field on the create-sandbox request body that selects the engine. `standard` is Firecracker (the default, no extra approval), `soma` is SOMA (needs an enabled policy and capacity), and `auto` lets policy decide and may pick Firecracker. Omitting the field is treated exactly as `standard`.

Related: Firecracker, SOMA, Sandbox, Runtime Profile

### Shared responsibility

Shared responsibility is the written split of who looks after what: MIOSA, you, or a cloud provider, depending on where your workload runs.

Read it before choosing infrastructure. With MIOSA-managed compute, MIOSA runs the machines. With OpenComputers, you own the hardware and OS. With BYOC, you own the cloud account and MIOSA runs the control plane.

In every model, the application owner owns application data and backup policy.

Related: MIOSA-managed infrastructure, Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC), OpenComputers

### SOMA

SOMA, the Secure Optimized Machine Architecture, is MIOSA's own open-source virtual machine monitor, written in Rust under Apache 2.0. It gives a Sandbox its own hardware-isolated Linux machine.

You do not run it. MIOSA operates SOMA for you, and it is in early access, enabled per Organization. It exists so MIOSA owns the exact moment a machine becomes ready to run commands.

In MIOSA, SOMA starts a sandbox by restoring a certified snapshot, then proves the guest is alive before calling it ready.

Related: Firecracker, Isolation, Sandbox, Snapshot, microVM, runtime_profile (sandbox field)

### Warm capacity

Warm capacity is compute kept ready in advance so a new Computer or Sandbox can start faster instead of cold booting.

It is why a managed Computer can be handed over in under a second on the warm path. It is not a guarantee that every size is available instantly.

In MIOSA, the managed fleet keeps ready desktop and sandbox slots on every host.

Related: Computer, Sandbox, MIOSA-managed Computer

### Worker pool

A Worker pool is a group of compatible hosts that may run a certain kind of workload under placement policy.

It gives MIOSA a set of machines to schedule onto. Mere registration is not enough: members must be compatible and able to do the job.

In MIOSA, a Bring Your Own Cloud region is a pool of worker capacity inside your AWS account or Google Cloud project.

Related: Host, Placement, Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC), Capability

integrations:
MIOSA gives you the full compute and preview infrastructure. You own the product, the brand, and the user relationship. Your customers never see "MIOSA".

This section covers everything you need to ship a white-label SaaS on top of MIOSA: per-user provisioning, custom domains, secure iframe embeds, webhooks, usage metering, and abuse controls.

---

## Core building blocks

- [Backend orchestration](/docs/integrations/backend-orchestration): Build the server-side control plane for prompt dispatch, device assignment, event streaming, artifact storage, and quota enforcement.
- [Fractal enterprise data](/docs/data/fractal): Run dedicated Fractal instances for massive-scale structured data and computation, secure and isolated for enterprise and government.
- [White-label SaaS walkthrough](/docs/platform/white-label): Provision customer-owned sandboxes, embed previews, use branded domains, and roll usage up to your users.
- [Preview tokens](/docs/develop/previews): Keep API keys server-side while safely embedding sandbox previews and customer-facing runtime surfaces.
- [Example apps](/docs/integrations/examples): Clone reference product patterns and adapt them to your own backend and frontend.

---

## What white-label tenants get

| Capability | What it means for your product |
|---|---|
| **Isolated sandboxes per user** | Each customer project runs in its own microVM with its own filesystem, network, and process tree. |
| **Custom preview domains** | Sandbox previews serve from `*.example.com` instead of `*.sandbox.miosa.ai`. |
| **Short-lived preview tokens** | Mint a server-side token, pass it to the browser  -  never expose your API key client-side. |
| **Webhook lifecycle events** | Receive `sandbox.running`, `sandbox.destroyed`, and more at your own HTTPS endpoint. |
| **Usage rollup by user** | Query compute usage keyed to your own `external_user_id` for per-seat billing. |
| **Per-user quotas** | Set max sandboxes, max CPU, or max runtime per user to prevent runaway spend. |
| **Branded failure pages** | 502 and 404 errors in previews show your logo, not MIOSA's. |
| **Full filesystem and terminal access** | Expose a file tree, terminal, or run-button in your UI using the SDK  -  no shell into MIOSA required. |

---

## Architecture patterns

Three deployment patterns cover the vast majority of integrations. All three keep your `msk_*` API key server-side.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph "Pattern 1  -  Server-side proxy"
    A1[Browser] -->|Your API routes| B1[Your backend]
    B1 -->|msk_ API key| C1[MIOSA API]
    B1 -->|Preview token| A1
    A1 -->|iframe src| D1[preview.miosa.ai / your domain]
  end

  subgraph "Pattern 2  -  Backend-for-Frontend (BFF)"
    A2[Browser] -->|REST/GraphQL| B2[BFF layer]
    B2 -->|msk_ API key| C2[MIOSA API]
    B2 -->|Short-lived JWT| A2
    A2 -->|SDK calls with JWT| C2
  end

  subgraph "Pattern 3  -  Direct with browser tokens"
    A3[Browser] -->|Auth request| B3[Your backend]
    B3 -->|Mint browser token| C3[MIOSA API]
    B3 -->|mp_ token| A3
    A3 -->|MIOSA SDK token| C3
  end
```

### Pattern 1  -  Server-side proxy (recommended for most teams)

Your backend owns all MIOSA calls. The browser only receives a short-lived preview URL from your API. This is the simplest pattern and the one used in the `whitelabel-saas` example.

**When to use:** You already have a backend. You want the tightest control over what each user can do. No SDK needed in the browser.

### Pattern 2  -  Backend-for-Frontend (BFF)

A thin BFF layer authenticates the user, resolves their MIOSA workspace/project IDs, and returns a short-lived JWT. The browser then calls MIOSA directly using that token.

**When to use:** High-volume preview-heavy products where round-tripping every terminal keystroke through your backend adds latency.

### Pattern 3  -  Direct with browser tokens

Your backend mints a scoped browser token (`mp_...`) once. The browser uses `@miosa/sdk` directly with that token for file reads, exec calls, and preview embeds.

**When to use:** Interactive coding tools or IDEs where the browser needs low-latency direct access to the sandbox.

1. [One-time setup](/docs/platform/white-label)  -  register your domain, set branding, configure a webhook
2. [Provision a sandbox per user](/docs/platform/white-label)  -  `client.sandboxes.create(external_user_id=...)`
3. [Embed the preview](/docs/platform/white-label)  -  mint a token server-side, drop an `<iframe>` in your UI

  [Examples gallery →](/docs/integrations/examples)

known-limitations:
We document what doesn't work, on purpose. If you hit something here, it isn't a bug in your code. It is a known gap. For release stages and the roadmap, see [Availability & Roadmap](/docs/availability); this page lists the concrete gaps and gotchas you can hit today.

> **Note**
>
> Last updated: 2026-10-11. We update this page on every release.

## Sandboxes `Public V1`

- **Availability is catalog-driven**. A named size, including `xs`, can be selected only when the template catalog and tenant policy admit it. A published contract is not a guarantee of immediate capacity in every environment.
- **The default is `small`**. It resolves to 2 vCPU, 4096 MiB RAM, and 10240 MiB disk. Raw CPU, memory, and disk fields must form a complete exact match for a published contract.
- **Timeouts are bounded**. `timeout_sec` defaults to 3600 and has a maximum of 86400. The extend endpoint replaces the timeout instead of adding duration. `always_on` is policy-dependent.
- **Usage can be incomplete**. Active CPU and network values can be `null` with `measurement_status` set to `unavailable`, or retained with status `stale`. Clients must not treat unavailable values as zero or stale values as current.
- **Snapshots are supported**. Public V1 includes customer-managed snapshot create, list, show, delete, and restore (`/sandboxes/{id}/snapshots` and `/sandboxes/{id}/restore/{snap_id}`), plus pause, resume, and fork.
- **AWS BYOC sandbox capacity is a gated private preview**. Managed and enabled BYOC environments share the sandbox contract, but BYOC placement is unavailable until the customer environment is accepted.
- **No GPU sandboxes**. The public sandbox create contract does not accept, persist, or schedule GPU requests; GPU runtime infrastructure exists behind a feature flag but is not productized, and no GPU rate is billable.
- **No nested virtualization**. KVM and QEMU cannot run inside a sandbox.

## Deployments `Phase 3/4 complete; dynamic runtime in hardening`

- **Custom domain apex records require ALIAS / ANAME**. DNS providers that do not support flattening, such as GoDaddy, require a workaround.
- **No edge functions yet**. Only origin compute is available.
- **Rollback is per-deployment, not per-route**. You cannot pin one URL path to version 1 and another to version 2 within the same deployment.
- **Containerized deployments publish through Docker Host**. Every sandbox ships Docker with the `docker compose` and `docker buildx` plugins, so you can build and test a container image there. A durable deployment of a containerized app is published through [Docker Host](/docs/docker-host/docker-deploy); the standard runtime builder builds from source and does not build OCI images into a deployment.
- **Railpack / Nixpacks framework detection** exists but dynamic generation from buildpacks is not complete.
- **Docker Host is a separate runtime path**. It publishes into the workspace Docker Host appliance and proves readiness through the `docker_deploy_app` row, container route, host health, and public URL. Standard MIOSA deployments and Docker Host deployments share the deployment API surface, but they do not use the same runtime substrate.

## Data Services

- **Managed Postgres** `Beta`. Provisioning lifecycle and credential injection exist. PgBouncer connection pooling and off-box backup drills are in progress.
- **Redis** `Beta`. Single-node only. Multi-zone replication is planned.
- **Object Storage** `Beta`. S3-compatible API is live; pre-signed browser uploads work. CDN distribution and geo-replication rollout are operational work in progress.
- **Auth-as-a-Service** `Beta`. Per-project email/password signup, login, JWT verify, password reset, and email confirmation endpoints are live. Refresh tokens, magic links, OAuth providers, MFA, and passkeys are still planned.
- **Volumes** `Beta`. Persistent local-backend volumes can be created, attached to computers, detached, deleted, and metered. Local volumes live on one host, so cross-host attach returns an error rather than moving the volume automatically.
- **Usage / audit query views grouped by `external_workspace_id`** have no API view. Raw audit events exist; aggregate them per workspace in your own code.

## Computers (Desktop) `GA`

- **Headed-only**: no headless mode for Computers. You boot a real Xfce desktop. For headless workloads, use Sandboxes.
- **Browser cookies do not persist** across sessions by default. Use a volume mount or browser profile snapshot to carry cookies across reboots.
- **No multi-monitor virtualization**. Single 1920 × 1080 frame buffer.
- **Audio not exposed**. The stream is video-only; system audio is dropped at the host.

## Computer-Use API

- **No managed agent loop**. You bring your own agent (Anthropic SDK, OpenAI computer-use API, or custom). A built-in `computer.prompt()` convenience will ship when the hosted Optimal session endpoint is publicly available.
- **Approval gating is not enforced server-side**. The approve / reject action protocol is a client-side convention only. Gate sensitive operations in your own agent code.
- **Computer sub-resources** (auto_stop, vnc_credentials, apps, stream_token, metrics, ports, volume attach/detach, clone) have full coverage in the Python SDK. TypeScript, Go, and Java parity is targeted Q3 2026.

## SDKs

| SDK | P1 + P2 resources | P3 / P4 resources | Computer depth |
|---|---|---|---|
| Python | Full | Full | Full |
| TypeScript | Full | Full | Partial |
| Go | Full | Partial | Partial |
| Java | Full | Partial | Partial |
| Elixir | Full | Partial | Partial |

- **Deployment proof parity is still uneven**. CLI, TypeScript SDK, Python SDK, and Go SDK expose proof checks. Java and Elixir proof helpers are still pending.
- **`embeddings`, `provider_defaults`, `benchmarks`, `command_center`, `community`, `email`, `builder_sessions`, `snapshots_standalone`** are Python-only today. Other SDK languages are pending.
- **Python sync client uses long-poll fallback** for streaming events. Use the async client or the TypeScript SDK for proper SSE.
- **Tab-synced language preference** persists in `localStorage`, not your user account. Switching language on one device does not propagate to another.

## API

- **No GraphQL endpoint**. REST + SSE by design.
- **Webhook delivery retries run for roughly 15.5 hours (within a 24-hour window)**. After eight attempts the event is dropped. Use the audit log to backfill missed events.
- **Rate limits**: 60 to 30,000 requests per minute per API key by tier, and 2,500/25,000/100,000 per minute per workspace on Developer/Business/Enterprise. Higher limits are available on request.
- **Browser tokens have a 1-hour default TTL** (60 seconds to 7 days). Refresh server-side; do not attempt client-side extension.
- **One sandbox per browser token**. A single token cannot scope across multiple sandboxes.

## Pricing and Billing

- **No per-tenant usage budgets yet**. You set a workspace cap today; tenant-level caps tied to `external_workspace_id` roll out with the billing attribution extension.
- **All traffic is billable** against the account’s spendable credit balance today. See [Availability & Roadmap](/docs/availability) for test-mode keys.

## Observability

- **No native log aggregation across workspaces**. Query per-resource today.
- **No OTLP trace export yet**. The `/events` SSE streams provide raw events; bring your own collector.

## See Also

- [Changelog](/docs/changelog) - what we just shipped
- [Concepts](/docs/concepts) - the resource model
- Contact platform@miosa.ai if a limitation here is blocking you. We prioritize the roadmap by demand.

machines:
A machine is the compute behind a sandbox or a computer: a versioned template, a named size, a runtime engine, and the tools already installed in the image.
Pick the closest template to your stack, choose a size, and MIOSA boots the machine ready to run your code.

## Templates

A **template** is a prebuilt sandbox image with a specific language, framework, or toolchain already installed.
Pick the closest match to your stack; you can override install/start commands per sandbox if needed.
See [Templates](/docs/develop/templates) for the built-in images and the custom BuildSpec reference.

## Sizes

Every sandbox runs on a named resource contract.
The default is `small`: 2 vCPU, 4096 MiB RAM, and 10240 MiB disk.
Prefer a named `size` over raw CPU, memory, and disk fields.
See [Sizing and limits](/docs/develop/sandboxes/sizing) for the contracts and what each costs.

## Runtimes

A sandbox runs on one of two engines: **Firecracker**, MIOSA's long-standing default, or **SOMA**, MIOSA's own open-source VMM.
Your organization chooses which runtimes it offers, and a sandbox records the runtime it was created with.
See [Choosing a runtime](/docs/soma/choosing-a-runtime) to list the runtimes you can pick and what each reports it supports today.

## Pre-installed tools

Templates ship with their toolchains already in the image, so there is nothing to install before your first command.
Docker with the `docker compose` and `docker buildx` plugins is available in every sandbox, including SOMA runtimes.

## Next

- [Templates](/docs/develop/templates): The built-in images and what each is prebuilt for, plus custom BuildSpecs.
- [Sizing and limits](/docs/develop/sandboxes/sizing): Named resource contracts, raw overrides, and billing notes.
- [Choosing a runtime](/docs/soma/choosing-a-runtime): Firecracker, SOMA, or auto, and how to list what your organization offers.
- [Sandboxes](/docs/develop/sandboxes): The full sandbox product: exec, files, previews, snapshots, and lifecycle.
mcp:
CLI & MCP

Give any AI client full MIOSA tools: OSA, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Hermes.

`{ "mcpServers": { "miosa": { "url": "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer msk_u_..." } } } }`

Every MIOSA tool inside OSA, our open-source agent, as mcp__miosa__* tools.

Save as ~/.osa/mcp.json, or run /mcp add inside OSA.

- [Install and authenticate](/docs/mcp/install): Hosted HTTP or local stdio, keys and organization context.
- [Use from agents](/docs/mcp#osa): Connect OSA, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or Hermes.
- [Tools reference](/docs/mcp/tools): All 151 tools, grouped by family.
- [CLI or MCP](/docs/cli/cli-vs-mcp): Which one to give an agent, and why both work.

MIOSA ships a public **Model Context Protocol** server. Point any MCP-aware client at it with an `msk_u_*` API key and you get the MIOSA toolbelt. [OSA](/docs/mcp#osa), MIOSA's open-source agent, is the primary client, and Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Hermes work the same way. The toolbelt: sandboxes, full GUI computers, snapshots, deployments, databases, storage, volumes, cron, functions, webhooks, API keys, workspaces, computer services, and regions.

This page is the server your own agent calls. For the other direction, the official tool servers you add to your agents, see the [tool server catalog](/docs/mcp/catalog).

Hosted endpoint:

```text
https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/mcp
```

The server speaks MCP 2025-03-26 Streamable HTTP, single-POST JSON-RPC. No SSE listen stream is required.

## OSA

OSA is MIOSA's open-source agent. It runs on your machine or on a MIOSA computer, and works with your Claude or ChatGPT subscription. It is an MCP client, so it takes the MIOSA server as another set of tools next to its built-ins; they appear as `mcp__miosa__*`.

Install OSA (macOS, Linux and Windows), then start it once to run the setup wizard:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Miosa-osa/OSA/main/scripts/install.sh | sh
osa
```

On Windows use `irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Miosa-osa/OSA/main/scripts/install.ps1 | iex`. Homebrew installs the `osagent` binary instead: `brew install Miosa-osa/homebrew-tap/osagent`.

Add MIOSA to `~/.osa/mcp.json` (user scope). The file uses the same `mcpServers` shape as Claude Desktop, and a `url` selects the HTTP transport:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "miosa": {
      "url": "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer msk_u_..." }
    }
  }
}
```

Or add it from inside OSA with the slash command, which writes the same file. OSA does not expand environment variables in `headers`, so put the key itself in the value:

```text
/mcp add miosa https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/mcp -t http -s user -H 'Authorization: Bearer msk_u_...'
```

Run `/mcp` to list servers and their connection status. A project `.mcp.json` also works; OSA asks for approval before it starts a project-scoped server.

## Claude Code

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http miosa \
  https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer msk_u_..."
```

Add `--scope user` to make it available across all your projects. Verify with `claude mcp list`.

Equivalently, in `.mcp.json` (project) or `~/.claude.json` (user):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "miosa": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer msk_u_..." }
    }
  }
}
```

## Codex

`~/.codex/config.toml`:

```toml
[mcp_servers.miosa]
url = "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/mcp"
bearer_token_env_var = "MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

`bearer_token_env_var` names the environment variable holding the key, not the key itself. The variable must be present in the environment that launches Codex. The one-line form:

```bash
codex mcp add miosa --url https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/mcp --bearer-token-env-var=MIOSA_API_KEY
```

## Cursor

`~/.cursor/mcp.json` (global) or `.cursor/mcp.json` (per project):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "miosa": {
      "url": "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer msk_u_..." }
    }
  }
}
```

## Hermes

[Hermes Agent](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent) is Nous Research's open-source agent. MCP support ships with the standard install. Add MIOSA to `~/.hermes/config.yaml`:

```yaml
mcp_servers:
  miosa:
    url: "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/mcp"
    headers:
      Authorization: "Bearer ${MIOSA_API_KEY}"
```

Hermes resolves `${MIOSA_API_KEY}` in `url` and `headers` when it connects, from the environment and from `~/.hermes/.env`, so the key stays out of the config file. Put `MIOSA_API_KEY=msk_u_...` in `~/.hermes/.env`, then start `hermes chat`.

## Claude Desktop

Claude Desktop's `claude_desktop_config.json` is stdio only. Use the `mcp-remote` bridge, which launches as a stdio server and proxies to the hosted endpoint.

`~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "miosa": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "-y",
        "mcp-remote",
        "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/mcp",
        "--header",
        "Authorization: Bearer ${MIOSA_API_KEY}"
      ],
      "env": { "MIOSA_API_KEY": "msk_u_..." }
    }
  }
}
```

Restart the app (not just reload) after editing. Alternatively, add the hosted URL under Settings, Connectors, Add custom connector and set the Authorization header there.

> **Note**
>
> Prefer the local stdio server (Python package) when you need to wrap the MCP layer with custom local logic, or your client does not support remote MCP. Both modes hit the same MIOSA REST API. See [Install and authenticate](/docs/mcp/install).

## Action authority

Governed MCP tools ask MIOSA's control-plane action authority immediately before dispatch. The control plane owns capability versions, grants, one-time approvals, revocation and receipts. The MCP server only maps tool names to canonical capabilities from a generated contract, and never copies policy locally.

Every registered tool has exactly one canonical capability. A tool with no mapping fails closed before any dispatch. Pending approval, denial, a missing catalog capability, or an unavailable authority all fail closed before the SDK or REST operation runs.

## Active computer

All computer tools accept an optional `computer_id`. When omitted, the server uses the most recently created or accessed computer, so you can `computer_create` once and omit the ID for the rest of the session.

## Errors

Failed tool calls use MCP `isError=true` and include a structured error object that preserves the backend error code, HTTP status, request ID, response details, tool name and a human-readable message. Clients can branch on stable codes such as `INVALID_TENANT_CONTEXT` without parsing display text.

- [Install and authenticate](/docs/mcp/install): Hosted HTTP and local stdio, keys, and tenant context.
- [Tools reference](/docs/mcp/tools): All 151 tools, grouped by family.
migrating-from-miosa-sandbox:
The standalone sandbox packages are deprecated compatibility wrappers. Each one now delegates to the canonical MIOSA SDK, so the fastest migration is often to install the canonical package and change one import.

| Deprecated package | Canonical replacement |
|---|---|
| `@miosa/sandbox` (JavaScript) | `@miosa/sdk` |
| `miosa-sandbox` (Python) | `miosa` |
| `sandboxes-go` (Go) | `github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa-go/v2` |

## JavaScript

```bash
npm install @miosa/sdk
```

```typescript
// Before
import { MIOSA } from '@miosa/sandbox';
const client = new MIOSA({ apiKey: process.env.MIOSA_API_KEY! });

// After
import { Miosa } from '@miosa/sdk';
const client = new Miosa({ apiKey: process.env.MIOSA_API_KEY! });
```

`@miosa/sandbox` re-exports the canonical client, so it keeps installing while you migrate, but new code should import `@miosa/sdk` directly. The renamed classes map as:

| Old import | Canonical replacement |
|---|---|
| `MIOSA` | `Miosa` |
| `SandboxClient` | `Sandboxes` |
| `ComputerClient` | `Computers` |
| `CreateSandboxOptions` | `SandboxCreateParams` |
| `CreateComputerOptions` | `ComputerCreateParams` |

## Python

```bash
pip install miosa
```

```python
# Before
from miosa_sandbox import MIOSA
with MIOSA(api_key="msk_...") as client:
    with client.sandboxes.create() as sandbox:
        print(sandbox.exec("python3 -c 'print(1 + 1)'").stdout)

# After
from miosa import Miosa
with Miosa(api_key="msk_...") as client:
    with client.sandboxes.create() as sandbox:
        print(sandbox.exec("python3 -c 'print(1 + 1)'").stdout)
```

`MIOSA` and `AsyncMIOSA` are preserved in the compatibility package and return the canonical `miosa` resource classes; the async class becomes `AsyncMiosa`.

## Go

```bash
go get github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa-go/v2
```

```go
// Before
import sandboxes "github.com/miosa-ai/sandboxes-go"
client, _ := sandboxes.New(sandboxes.Config{APIKey: os.Getenv("MIOSA_API_KEY")})

// After
import miosa "github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa-go/v2"
client := miosa.NewClient("msk_...")
```

> **Note: Sunset window**
>
> The `sandboxes-go` package receives bug fixes but no new features, with a sunset date of 2026-11-08. The JavaScript and Python compatibility packages exist only so older integrations keep installing while they migrate.

## Behavior differences to expect

- **One client, one surface.** In the canonical SDKs, sandboxes live on the client (`client.sandboxes`) alongside computers, files, snapshots, and agent runs. Code that reached for a separate sandbox client now goes through the single client.
- **Ownership selectors are first-class.** `workspace_id`, `project_id`, and `external_user_id` can be passed directly on create, and are exposed on the returned handle.
- **`size` and `resource_contract`.** When no size is supplied, the compatibility packages request the canonical `small` contract: 2 vCPU, 4096 MiB memory, and 10240 MiB disk. The response exposes `size`, `resource_contract`, and `usage()` on both sync and async handles.
- **Canonical names.** Use `client.sandboxes` on the sandbox image, `client.computers` with `miosa-desktop`, and `client.dockerDeploy` for the Docker Host appliance. `computer` is the user-facing product name; `miosa-desktop` is the template it boots from.

## Verify the migration

The compatibility packages and the canonical SDKs hit the same API, so the check is behavioral:

```python
from miosa import Miosa

with Miosa(api_key="msk_...") as client:
    sbx = client.sandboxes.create(template_id="miosa-sandbox", size="small")
    print(sbx.state, sbx.resource_contract)
    print(sbx.exec("python3 -c 'print(1 + 1)'").stdout)   # 2
    sbx.destroy()
```

If that prints `2` and a `small` contract, the migration is complete.

## See also

- [TypeScript SDK](/docs/sdks/typescript): The canonical JavaScript and TypeScript client.
- [Python SDK](/docs/sdks/python): The canonical Python client, sync and async.
- [Go SDK](/docs/sdks/go): The canonical Go client, version 2.

optimal-engine:
Optimal Engine is a memory and knowledge engine for a person, a team, or a company.
It keeps the sources you give it, turns them into memory that someone has reviewed, and returns cited context to people and agents.
It is open source under the Apache 2.0 license, at [github.com/Miosa-osa/OptimalEngine](https://github.com/Miosa-osa/OptimalEngine).

Optimal Engine is not the Optimal chat agent.
[Optimal](/docs/optimal) is the agent you chat with in the console.
Optimal Engine is the store it remembers with: a server you run yourself, or a managed one on MIOSA.

## What it does

| Step | What the Engine does |
|---|---|
| Organize | Keeps a tree of organizations, workspaces, and typed nodes such as people, products, and projects |
| Capture | Stores raw text, files, chat sessions, Notion exports, and records pulled from apps such as Slack, GitHub, and Linear |
| Remember | Classifies each input, extracts claims, and promotes a claim to a fact only after review or a confidence rule |
| Retrieve | Searches with full-text ranking, adds vector search when an embedding model is set up, and returns context with its sources |
| Operate | Gives agents a daily brief, open loops, a protocol, and allow, ask, or deny rules for what they may do |
| Project | Writes the same state out as markdown files, wiki pages, workspace bundles, and an HTTP API |

The Engine does not write answers with a language model.
`ask` returns the context and the sources an answer should come from, and your agent or model writes the answer.

## Two ways to run it

| | Self-hosted | On MIOSA |
|---|---|---|
| Where it runs | Your machine, server, or container | A private machine in your MIOSA workspace |
| Who runs it | You: install, keys, backups, upgrades | MIOSA: provisioning, backups, upgrades, health checks |
| Search | Full-text, plus vector search with your own embedding model | Full-text |
| How you reach it | `http://127.0.0.1:4200` or your own domain | The **Memory** page, Optimal chat, the `miosa engine` commands, and machines in the workspace |
| Availability | Anyone, from the repository | Enabled per organization |

Self-hosting needs nothing from MIOSA.
See the [self-hosted quickstart](/docs/optimal-engine/quickstart) or [Optimal Engine on MIOSA](/docs/optimal-engine/miosa).

> **Note: Current release**
>
> These pages describe Optimal Engine 0.3.10, API version `v1`.
> Check what a running Engine reports with `GET /api/version`.

## Where to go next

- [Concepts](/docs/optimal-engine/concepts): Workspaces, nodes, sources, claims, facts, and context packages.
- [Quickstart](/docs/optimal-engine/quickstart): Run an Engine, store a source, and search it in about ten minutes.
- [Install and configure](/docs/optimal-engine/install): Requirements, Docker, settings, storage, and API keys.
- [Memory and retrieval](/docs/optimal-engine/memory-and-retrieval): How search, ask, and the review of claims work.
- [API reference](/docs/optimal-engine/api): Authentication, errors, and the main routes with examples.
- [Optimal Engine on MIOSA](/docs/optimal-engine/miosa): Workspace Memory, managed Engines, and keys for the CLI.
optimal:
Optimal is MIOSA's built-in agent.
You describe what you want in a chat, and Optimal answers from your live workspace, builds on a machine you choose, or investigates a problem.
Open it from **Optimal** in the console sidebar, at `/optimal`.

## What Optimal does

- **Answers** questions about your organization and workspace: what is running, what changed, how something is set up.
- **Builds** on a sandbox or computer: it writes files, runs commands, serves a live preview, and can publish what it built.
- **Investigates** a problem: it traces evidence, such as a failed deployment or an error in your logs, before it reaches a conclusion.
- **Asks before it acts**: steps that change your workspace wait for your approval unless you allow them.

Optimal works only inside your organization and workspace, with your permissions.
See [Isolation and permissions](/docs/optimal/isolation).

## Brains: who does the work

Before the first message you pick the brain that answers the chat.

| Brain | Who pays | What runs |
|---|---|---|
| Optimal | Wallet credits | MIOSA's own model, with a 1M-token context |
| A harness | Your own account | Claude Code, Codex, OSA, and the other harnesses run on a machine |
| A saved agent | Your own account | An agent you built in Agent Studio, with its own instructions and tools |

The brain is locked after the first message.
To change it, start a new chat.
See [Brains and agents](/docs/optimal/brains).

## Ask, Build, Investigate

Every chat is in one of three modes.

| Mode | What it does |
|---|---|
| Ask | Answers from live workspace context, without touching a machine |
| Build | Builds or changes something on a sandbox or computer |
| Investigate | Traces evidence before reaching a conclusion |

Investigate always runs on the Optimal brain.
See [Chats and modes](/docs/optimal/chats).

## Pricing in one line

The Optimal brain costs $1.90 per 1M input tokens and $8.00 per 1M output tokens, paid from wallet credits where 1 credit is 1 cent.
A typical message is about 3 credits.
Machines Optimal uses are billed at their normal rate.
A harness or saved agent bills its model to your own account.
See [Pricing and usage](/docs/optimal/pricing).

## Where to go next

- [Quickstart](/docs/optimal/quickstart): Your first chat, first build, and first API call.
- [Chats and modes](/docs/optimal/chats): The composer, attachments, context, and chat history.
- [Build on your machines](/docs/optimal/machines): Pick a machine, use the side panel, and take over.
- [Approvals](/docs/optimal/approvals): What Optimal asks before it acts, and how to allow it.
- [Optimal API](/docs/optimal/api): Create chats, send messages, and stream replies over HTTP.
- [Troubleshooting](/docs/optimal/troubleshooting): Credits, machines, and errors, with fixes.
plans-and-limits:
There are four plans.
Every plan pays the same published price for a size.
Plans differ in what they include and in how much you can run.

| Plan | Price | Included usage each month | Past the included usage |
|---|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | $1 | Stops at $1. Add credits to keep going. |
| Developer | $20/mo | $20 | Pay as you go. Add credits any time. |
| Business | $500/mo | $500 | Pay as you go. Add credits any time. |
| Enterprise | $2,000/mo | $2,000 | Pay as you go, invoiced |

Pick a plan in [Billing](https://miosa.ai/billing).
Free works for a first try.

## Per service

A service's replicas, size and storage are limited by your plan.

| Plan | Replicas | Largest replica | All replicas together | Always-on | Volume | Image |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Free | 1 | 1 vCPU, 0.5 GB | 0.5 GB, 1 vCPU | No, it sleeps | 0.5 GB | 4 GB |
| Free with added credits | 2 | 2 vCPU, 2 GB | 2 GB, 2 vCPU | No, it sleeps | 2 GB | 8 GB |
| Developer | 4 | 4 vCPU, 8 GB | 16 GB, 8 vCPU | Yes | 10 GB | 20 GB |
| Business | 10 | 8 vCPU, 16 GB | 64 GB, 32 vCPU | Yes | 250 GB | 50 GB |
| Enterprise | 20 | 16 vCPU, 32 GB | 128 GB, 64 vCPU | Yes | 1 TB | Unlimited |

## Per account

These totals count everything running at once: services, sandboxes, computers and databases.

| Plan | Running memory | Running vCPU | Projects | Sandboxes | Computers | Databases | Egress per month | Seats |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Free | 2 GB | 2 | 1 | 1 (stops after 30 minutes) | 1 small, hibernates after 15 idle minutes | 1 small | 5 GB | 1 |
| Free with added credits | 6 GB | 4 | 2 | 2 (stop after 2 hours) | 1, up to 2 vCPU and 4 GB | 2 | 20 GB | 1 |
| Developer | 32 GB | 16 | 10 | 5 | 3 | 5 | 100 GB | 1 |
| Business | 128 GB | 64 | Unlimited | 25 | 20 | 25 | 1 TB | 10 |
| Enterprise | 256 GB | 128 | Unlimited | 100 | 100 | 100 | 5 TB | Unlimited |

Enterprise totals can be raised by agreement.

## Free with added credits

A Free account can add credits, from $5.
Added credits never expire.
While the added balance is above $0, the "Free with added credits" limits apply.
When it reaches $0, the account is back on the Free limits.

## Dedicated vCPU

Dedicated vCPU sizes are for Business and Enterprise.
See [Dedicated vCPU](/docs/services/dedicated-vcpu).

## When you reach a limit

A create or a deploy that would pass a limit is refused with an error that names the limit and the plan that raises it.
Nothing running is stopped.
Your limits and usage are in [Billing](https://miosa.ai/billing).

## Guardrails

Two limits sit above the plan tables, and both are there to keep the fleet honest:

- **Running memory per organization.** No organization runs more than about
  100 GB of memory at once without an administrator override, whatever its plan.
- **Fleet pressure.** When the committed memory on the fleet passes 80% of what
  is free, new Free creates pause and new Free signups queue until capacity
  returns. Paid creates continue. Nothing already running is stopped.

## Where to go next

- [Pricing](/docs/pricing): the per-size rates every plan pays.
- [Credits](/docs/api-reference/credits): how credits are bought, spent and expire.
pricing:
What a sandbox costs per hour, what a plan buys, how many sandboxes you can run and start, and how that compares to other providers.

Every size has one price per hour. You pay it per second, and only while a sandbox or computer is running.
A paused, stopped or destroyed sandbox costs nothing for compute, and the price does not change with how busy the machine is.
Storage is metered on its own: disk costs $0.09 per GiB-month while the machine runs, and paused disk, named snapshots, and backups cost $0.018 per GiB-month. Buckets and static sites cost $0.0162 per GiB-month.
One credit is always one US cent.
Each organization keeps 10 named snapshots included; each one after that is $1.70 a month.
There are no other discounts, bonuses or free allowances: egress is billed from the first GB. Builds are free.

## Price

| Size | Per hour | Always on (730 h) | CPU | RAM | Disk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `micro` | $0.0316 | $23.05 | 1 vCPU | 0.5 GiB | 10 GiB |
| `tiny` | $0.0359 | $26.22 | 1 vCPU | 1 GiB | 20 GiB |
| `xs` | $0.0446 | $32.58 | 1 vCPU | 2 GiB | 10 GiB |
| `small` | $0.0893 | $65.16 | 2 vCPU | 4 GiB | 10 GiB |
| `quad` | $0.1437 | $104.90 | 4 vCPU | 4 GiB | 20 GiB |
| `medium` | $0.1785 | $130.32 | 4 vCPU | 8 GiB | 20 GiB |
| `large` | $0.3570 | $260.65 | 8 vCPU | 16 GiB | 40 GiB |
| `xl` | $0.7141 | $521.29 | 16 vCPU | 32 GiB | 80 GiB |

- The price is the size: it is the same whether the machine is idle or fully busy, and it is charged per second while the machine runs.
- Disk is provisioned, not used: you pay for the disk the size allocates, whether or not it is filled, at the storage rates above.
- `small` is the default size.
- Every size is a full machine with the same features, templates, and API. Only the resources change.
- Computers (desktops) come in `xs` through `xl`. A computer costs exactly what a sandbox of the same size costs: `xs` $0.0446 an hour, `small` $0.0893, `medium` $0.1785, `large` $0.3570, `xl` $0.7141. Their disks are larger: `xs` 10 GiB, `small` 20 GiB, `medium` 40 GiB, `large` 80 GiB, `xl` 160 GiB.

Apps and databases are billed on what they use, and never more than the price of their size in this table.
A small app that sits idle most of the day pays far less than the table; a busy one pays the table price at most.
Egress is $0.054 per GB, with no free allowance.
Deployment builds are free.
Your plan sets the largest size you can pick, never the price.

## Apps, services and databases

Apps, services and databases are billed on what they use, per second, and never more than the price of their size.

| What | Price |
|---|---|
| CPU actually busy | $21.915 per vCPU-month |
| Memory actually used | $10.953 per GiB-month |
| Idle CPU, unused memory, a stopped service | not billed |
| Most you can pay for a size, per second while it runs | the size price in the table above (`xs` $0.0446 an hour, `small` $0.0893, `medium` $0.1785, `large` $0.3570, `xl` $0.7141) |

- A small app that sits idle most of the day pays far less than its size price; a busy one pays the size price at most. The size is the cap, not the bill.
- Managed databases follow the same rule on their own sizes (never more than the sandbox price of the same size), plus disk at $0.162 per GiB-month.
- Running disk is $0.09 per GiB-month and egress $0.054 per GB. Builds are free.
- `GET /api/v1/pricing` lists each size under `products.machines.app.sizes` and `products.machines.database.sizes` with `usd_per_hour` and `usd_per_month`, and `price_kind` `maximum`.

## Plans and concurrency

| Plan | Price | Included usage each month |
|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | $1 |
| Developer | $20/mo | $20 |
| Business | $500/mo | $500 |
| Enterprise | $2,000/mo | $2,000 |

Limits per service and per account are on [Plans and limits](/docs/plans-and-limits).

- The plan price comes back as usage: Business is $500 for $500 of usage, and every credit spends at the prices above.
- Plans never change the price of a size, only the caps.
- Top up any time from $1 to $5,000. Purchased credits never expire; recurring plan credits expire a month after they are granted.
- Start free with $1 of usage every month. Paid plans pay as you go. Free stops at its $1 unless you buy credits. Add credits any time.
- When your balance reaches $0, running computers and sandboxes pause and resume on their own when you add credit; databases and deployments are stopped and may need a manual restart after you add credit. Nothing is deleted. New machines start only while you have credit.
- Starting a sandbox is an API call, so it is rate-limited per API key (60 to 30,000 requests per minute by tier) and per plan. See [Rate limits](/docs/rate-limits).

## Get started

- [Create a free account](https://miosa.ai/register): Free includes $1 of usage every month. No card needed.
- [Pick a plan](https://miosa.ai/billing): Free works for a first try. Choose or change your plan in Billing.

Already signed up? [Sign in](https://miosa.ai/login).

## Limits

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Concurrent sandboxes | See [Plans and limits](/docs/plans-and-limits) |
| Sandbox lifetime (`timeout_sec`) | 1 to 86,400 seconds, default 3,600 |
| Idle auto-pause | 30 minutes for accounts created on or after October 11, 2026; wakes on the next request |
| Exec | 30 seconds per call by default; detached jobs have no limit |
| Run code (`/code/run`) | 300 seconds maximum |
| File upload | 500 MB per write |
| Browser token | 1 hour by default, 60 seconds to 7 days |
| Named snapshots | 10 free per organization, then $1.70 a month each |

Cap one of your own end users, below the organization limit, with the [Quotas API](/docs/api-reference/quotas) (`max_sandboxes`, `max_concurrent`, `max_storage_gb`, `max_credit_cents`).

## Compared to others

The same machine, **4 vCPU and 8 GiB of RAM, running**, at each provider's public list price, checked 2026-10-20.
Each price is followed by its multiplier against MIOSA.

| Provider | 4 vCPU + 8 GiB / hour | vs MIOSA |
|---|---|---|
| **MIOSA** | **$0.1785** | **1x** |
| Railway | $0.2223 | 1.2x |
| Freestyle | $0.2645 | 1.5x |
| E2B | $0.3312 | 1.9x |
| Vercel † | $0.6816 | 3.8x |

† Bills active CPU, not allocated CPU.

MIOSA's figure is compute only; disk is metered separately at the rate above.
Several providers meter storage and egress on top of compute, so a real monthly bill can differ from the compute line.

MIOSA is below every provider listed here for this machine.
For capabilities and measured performance, see [MIOSA vs other platforms](/docs/compare) and the [compute provider comparison](/docs/integrations/comparison).

Sources, each checked 2026-10-20: [Freestyle](https://www.freestyle.sh/pricing), [E2B](https://e2b.dev/pricing), [Railway](https://railway.com/pricing), [Vercel Sandbox](https://vercel.com/docs/vercel-sandbox/pricing).

### Why some providers list a lower hourly price

Most sandbox providers sell the machine, and that is where their product ends.
You then stitch together other services for hosting, databases, agents, tenants and billing.

MIOSA prices the machine as part of a whole platform, so one account covers what you need to build and run a full-stack, multi-tenant application:

- [Deployments and Docker Host](/docs/docker-host/overview) to publish what you build to a stable URL with your own domain, versions and rollback.
- [Agents](/docs/guides/agent-operating-guide) with harnesses and approvals, running inside your machines.
- [Managed data](/docs/data/overview): Postgres, Redis, MySQL and Qdrant.
- [Organizations, workspaces and the white-label kit](/docs/platform/overview) to run it for your own team or sell it as your product.

If you only need a raw sandbox and nothing around it, a sandbox-only provider may fit.
If you want to build, deploy and run a product on one platform, that is where MIOSA's value is.

## Performance

MIOSA in the independent ComputeSDK benchmark suite. Every run is a committed JSON file, so each number can be checked against the repository.

| Benchmark | MIOSA | Field | Date |
|---|---|---|---|
| Burst startup: 100 concurrent creates, timed to the first command | 57.09 ms median | #1 of 32 | 2026-10-23 |
| DAX build: clone, install, typecheck in a fresh sandbox | 38.4 s | #1 of 16 completed | 2026-08-21 |
| DAX build, latest completed run | 39.2 s | #2 of 20 | 2026-10-02 |

See [Benchmarks](/docs/benchmarks) for every run and the raw results.
A cost per run is not published, because the benchmark sandbox size is not part of the result; size a run from the rates in [Worked examples](/docs/pricing#worked-examples).

## Worked examples

| You run | Per month |
|---|---|
| 1 `small` sandbox, 2 hours a day (60 h) | 60 x $0.089262 = **$5.36** |
| 1 `small` sandbox, always on (730 h) | 730 x $0.089262 = **$65.16** |
| 1 `medium` sandbox, 8 hours a day (176 h) | 176 x $0.178524 = **$31.42** |
| 1 `large` sandbox, always on (730 h) | 730 x $0.357048 = **$260.65** |
| 10,000 one-minute jobs on `small` | 166.7 h x $0.089262 = **$14.88** |
| 10 GiB kept paused for a month | 10 x $0.018 = **$0.18** |
| 10 GiB of disk on a running `small` sandbox, always on (730 h) | 10 x $0.09 = **$0.90**, on top of the $65.16 |

Compute for these examples only; running disk is metered on top at $0.09 per GiB-month.

## For the API

- `GET /api/v1/pricing` returns the price book this page is built from: for each product a list of sizes with `usd_per_hour` and `usd_per_month` (730 hours), the per-resource rates, and the plans. Sandboxes and computers have `price_kind: "flat"`; apps and databases have `price_kind: "maximum"`, the most they can cost for that size. `GET /api/v1/compute/pricing` serves the same body.
- `GET /api/v1/credits/balance` reports the balance in credits, with lifetime earned, lifetime spent, and the nearest expiry. One credit is $0.01, so 100 credits is $1.00.
- A sandbox or computer is billed the price of its size per second while it runs, with a 1-second minimum, and settled against the balance every 5 minutes. Apps and databases are billed on measured CPU and memory use, capped per second at the price of their size.
- The [Usage Rollup API](/docs/api-reference/usage-rollup) aggregates by `external_user_id`, `external_project_id`, or `workspace_id`, so a rollup maps onto your own billing.

> **Tip: One price per size for every plan**
>
> Every plan pays the same price for a size. Plans only change the caps and the concurrency, never the price.

## MIOSA AI pricing

MIOSA AI bills in wallet credits where 1 credit is 1 cent.

projects:
A **Project** is the durable product boundary inside one Workspace.
It groups the resources for one application, site, workflow, or customer deliverable, and it never runs code itself.
Every resource that belongs to the product carries the project's `project_id`, so ownership, deployment history, domains, members, and usage all roll up to one boundary.

A Project always belongs to exactly one Workspace, and a Workspace belongs to one Organization.
The Workspace is required: creating a Project with no workspace fails with `WORKSPACE_REQUIRED`.

## 1. Create a project

```bash
miosa project create "Lead Magnet" \
  --workspace-id "$MIOSA_WORKSPACE_ID" \
  --description "Customer lead capture app"

miosa project list
miosa project get lead-magnet
```

## 2. Add resources

```bash
# Create a sandbox in the workspace, then publish its output.
miosa create lead-magnet-dev --workspace acme-corp --wait
miosa deploy create --from-sandbox lead-magnet-dev --wait
```

## 3. Deploy

```bash
miosa deploy create --git https://github.com/me/lead-magnet --branch main --wait
```

Publishing creates an immutable version under the Deployment and prints the URL.
Display the URL the API returns; never rebuild it from a slug.

rate-limits:
MIOSA rate-limits API requests per API key, per workspace, and per endpoint group. When you exceed a limit, the API returns HTTP `429` with a `Retry-After` header telling you how many seconds to wait before retrying.

This page covers request throttling only. Hard caps that are not about request rate - concurrent sandboxes, exec and upload limits, webhook retries, browser token TTL - and everything billable live on [Pricing and limits](/docs/pricing).

## Request limits

| Scope | Limit |
|---|---|
| Per API key | 60 to 30,000 requests per minute, depending on the key's tier |
| Per workspace | Your plan's public-API limit, in requests per minute: Developer 2,500, Business 25,000, Enterprise 100,000 |
| Per endpoint group | Static per-minute caps per endpoint family (for example 30,000 on the public API and 3,000 on event streams) |
| All `/egress/*` endpoints | Current limit returned in `X-RateLimit-*` headers |

Limits can vary by key and policy. Every response carries the current numbers in `X-RateLimit-*` headers, so read them rather than hardcoding the values above.

> **Tip: Higher limits on request**
>
> Contact support to raise a request limit for a heavy integration. Volume terms are negotiated per plan; see the [pricing page](https://miosa.ai/pricing).

## Handle a 429

```python
import time, requests

def call(url, **kwargs):
    while True:
        res = requests.get(url, **kwargs)
        if res.status_code != 429:
            return res
        time.sleep(int(res.headers.get("Retry-After", "1")))
```

Back off for the number of seconds in `Retry-After`, then retry. Do not retry in a tight loop; `429` is a signal to slow down, not to try harder.

On the opt-in runner endpoint there are two distinct `429`s: `rate_limited` is the per-key or per-tenant limit, and `runtime_busy` (with `Retry-After: 0`) means the runner is at its admission limit and you should retry the request.

## See also

- [Pricing and limits](/docs/pricing): Billable states, machine sizes, hard caps, and per-end-user quotas.
- [Errors](/docs/api-reference/errors): Error codes and the response envelope, including rate-limit errors.
- [Quotas API](/docs/api-reference/quotas): Cap a single end-user without touching the tenant limit.
regions:
Every Computer and every Sandbox is created in exactly one region and stays there for its lifetime. A resource does not span regions, and there is no live migration between them today.

## Available regions

| Slug | Location | City | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| `us-west` | US West | Los Angeles, CA | Live |
| `us-east` | US East | New York, NY | Live |
| `us-mia` | US East 2 | Miami | Live |

All three are generally available and none is restricted. A Computer defaults to your workspace's default region, or `us-mia` when none is set; a Sandbox has no default region and is placed wherever capacity allows.

## Pin a resource to a region

Pass `region` on create; the same field works on Computers and Sandboxes.

**Python**

```python
computer = client.computers.create(name="ny-build-box", size="M", region="us-east")
print(computer.region)   # "us-east"
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const computer = await client.computers.create({ name: 'ny-build-box', size: 'M', region: 'us-east' });
```

If you omit `region`, a Computer uses your workspace's default region (falling back to `us-mia`), while a Sandbox is placed wherever capacity allows; the response includes the resolved region when one is set. You can change your workspace's default region in dashboard settings; the override applies to Computer creation that omits the field.

| Status | Error | Cause |
|---|---|---|
| 400 | `invalid_region` | Slug not in the list above |
| 503 | `REGION_UNAVAILABLE` | Transient capacity issue; retry or pick another |

## List regions

**`GET /api/v1/regions`** returns the regions available to your tenant, so a region picker in your UI does not need a hardcoded list.

```bash
curl https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/regions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

Each entry has `id` (the region slug), `label`, `active_nodes`, `available`, `small_slots_free`, and a `headroom` object with free slots per size and the region's total and used memory. See the [Regions API](/docs/api-reference/regions) for the full response shape.

## What is region-local

- **Compute.** The VM runs in one region. All VM sizes are available in every region for both Computers and Sandboxes.
- **Data.** Data services and volumes live in the region of the resource that uses them.
- **Latency.** The three US sites are roughly equidistant for the median US user, so compute performance is effectively identical. Pick by data residency first; otherwise pick by proximity to your users or CI runners, which lowers RTT for desktop streaming and terminal round-trips.

## Cross-region

There is no live migration between regions. To run work in more than one region, create one resource per region, and federate bring-your-own hosts with [OpenComputers](/docs/api-reference/open-computers) if you want a single logical workspace across them.

EU and APAC regions are on the roadmap and will appear in `GET /api/v1/regions` alongside the current three.

> **Note: Regions are not runner endpoints**
>
> A resource's region (`us-west`, `us-east`, `us-mia`) is separate from the opt-in runner endpoint that serves fast create and exec calls. Region is about where the VM lives; the runner endpoint is about how your request reaches MIOSA. See [regions and the runner](/docs/develop/sandboxes/sizing) for that distinction.

- [Regions API](/docs/api-reference/regions): Request and response shapes for region listing and errors.
- [Sizing and limits](/docs/develop/sandboxes/sizing): Named resource contracts and the opt-in runner fast path.
sandboxes-or-computers:
Most work starts in a **Sandbox**.
Reach for a **Computer** when someone has to see and use a real screen.
When the result should stay online for your users, publish it with **Docker Host**.

- [Sandbox](/docs/develop/sandboxes): A fast, isolated machine for code. Run commands, edit files, install packages, open a live preview URL, and drive the built-in browser. Pauses when idle and wakes on the next request.
- [Computer](/docs/computers/overview): A durable cloud desktop. A real Linux screen with a browser, desktop apps, mouse and keyboard control, a live view a person can take over, and state that stays between sessions.

**Ready to go live?** [Docker Host](/docs/docker-host/docker-deploy) keeps what you built online at a stable URL, with your own domain, versions and rollback.

## Pick by what you need

| You want to | Use |
|---|---|
| Run code, build, test, or install packages | Sandbox |
| Show a live preview of an app while you build it | Sandbox |
| Let an agent browse and fill forms in a browser | Sandbox, with its [built-in browser](/docs/browser-use) |
| Use desktop apps, or anything that needs a full screen | Computer |
| Keep logins, files and a desktop around for days | Computer |
| Let a person watch and take over an agent's screen | Either: the sandbox browser or the computer desktop both have a live view |
| Keep an app online for your users | Docker Host |

> **Tip: Not sure? Start with a Sandbox**
>
> Sandboxes start fastest and cost the least.
> Move to a Computer only when the work truly needs a desktop.

## Create one

**CLI**

```bash
# A sandbox for code and previews
miosa create

# A computer with a full desktop
miosa computer create --size small
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { Miosa } from "@miosa/sdk";

const miosa = new Miosa({ apiKey: process.env.MIOSA_API_KEY! });

const sandbox = await miosa.sandboxes.create({ templateId: "miosa-sandbox" });
const computer = await miosa.computers.create({ name: "research-desk", size: "small" });
```

## Often you use both

A typical agent product writes and runs code in a Sandbox, uses a Computer when a task needs a real desktop, and publishes the finished app with Docker Host.
See [Agent device selection](/docs/guides/agent-device-selection) for the full decision guide, including when an agent needs no machine at all.

security:
Every MIOSA Sandbox and Computer ships with a built-in security boundary. **No setup. No add-on SKU. Free on every plan.**

Three things you can use whenever you need them:

| Feature | What it does | Page |
|---|---|---|
| **Secrets** | Store your API keys in MIOSA  -  sandboxes see opaque placeholders, the real values stay encrypted at rest | [Secrets](/docs/security/secrets) |
| **Connect Accounts** | OAuth-based credential connection (GitHub, Google, Slack, …) instead of pasting raw tokens | [Connect Accounts](/docs/security/connect-accounts) |
| **Network Allowlist** | Watch what your sandbox calls; lock it down to an approved list when you're ready | [Network](/docs/security/network) |
| **Audit Log** | Outbound calls recorded to the egress audit log  -  searchable, exportable, live-tail (capture is not yet enabled in the current release) | [Audit Log](/docs/security/audit-log) |

## Getting started in 60 seconds

Nothing to install. Nothing to configure globally. Each Computer / Sandbox already has the three tabs.

### 1. Add a credential

Open any Sandbox or Computer → **Secrets** tab → **+ Add Secret**

```text
Name:         openai_key
Value:        sk-proj-...   ← your real key
Expose as:    OPENAI_API_KEY
```

Or via SDK (Python  -  same shape in TypeScript / Go / Java / Elixir):

```python
sandbox.secrets.set(
    name="openai_key",
    value="sk-proj-...",
    expose_as_env="OPENAI_API_KEY",
)
```

Inside the sandbox, `process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY` is now an opaque `miosa-tok-…` placeholder. Your existing code uses it as normal. The real key is swapped in at the network boundary on the way out.

→ Full walkthrough: [Secrets](/docs/security/secrets)

### 2. Use your code unchanged

```python
import os, requests

requests.post(
    "https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['OPENAI_API_KEY']}"},
    json={...},
)
```

That's it. OpenAI sees your real `sk-…`. Your sandbox never does. No code change.

### 3. (Optional) Check what you called + lock it down

After your sandbox has been running for a while:

- **Audit Log tab**  -  live-tail outbound calls. Filter by host, status, time. Egress audit capture is not yet enabled in the current release.
- **Network tab**  -  see the auto-built list of hosts you've contacted. One click to enforce-mode with that list as the allowlist.

Both are opt-in. Audit-only is the default until you decide to lock down.

→ See [Network Allowlist](/docs/security/network) for the lockdown workflow.

### Want to wire up GitHub / Google / Slack instead of pasting tokens?

→ [Connect Accounts](/docs/security/connect-accounts)  -  OAuth flow that handles refresh automatically.

### Building a white-label product on top of MIOSA?

Your end-users don't need MIOSA accounts  -  credentials can be scoped to your own `external_user_id`.

→ [White-label Credentials](/docs/security/white-label)

## Your code doesn't change

The whole design rule for MIOSA Security: **your existing code keeps working.**

```python
import os, requests

# This code is identical with or without MIOSA Secrets:
response = requests.post(
    "https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['OPENAI_API_KEY']}"},
    json={...},
)
```

What changes is *the value* of `OPENAI_API_KEY`. Without Secrets, it's your real `sk-...` key. With Secrets, it's an opaque placeholder like `miosa-tok-7f2a8c...`. The MIOSA proxy substitutes the real key on the way out. OpenAI sees the real key. Your sandbox never does.

## Three guarantees

> **Note: Audit-only by default**
>
> New sandboxes do not block anything. The proxy watches and logs but never gets in the way. You only enter "enforce" mode by explicitly clicking Lock Down  -  and it's reversible in one click.

> **Note: Secrets stay encrypted**
>
> Once saved, secret values are encrypted with ChaCha20-Poly1305. They are unsealed only at the moment the proxy needs to swap them into an outbound request. Nobody  -  including MIOSA engineers  -  can re-read a stored value via the API or UI.

> **Note: Existing patterns still work**
>
> `.env` files still work. `tenant_provider_keys` and `workspace_env_vars` still work. MIOSA Secrets adds a new layer; it doesn't replace anything that exists today.

## Where to go next

- **First time using this?** Start with [Secrets  -  Quickstart](/docs/security/secrets).
- **Want to wire up OAuth (GitHub etc.)?** Read [Connect Accounts](/docs/security/connect-accounts).
- **Want to lock down outbound traffic?** Read [Network Allowlist](/docs/security/network).
- **Building a white-label product on MIOSA?** Read [White-label Credentials](/docs/security/white-label).

## Glossary

**Placeholder token**
An opaque string (format: `miosa-tok-<hex>`) that MIOSA injects into a sandbox's environment in place of a real credential. The proxy swaps the placeholder with the real value on every outbound request. The placeholder is unique per binding  -  it cannot be brute-forced to discover the real key.

**OAuth Connect**
A MIOSA feature that lets you authorize a third-party account (GitHub, Google, Slack, …) via the standard OAuth 2.0 flow instead of pasting a static API key. MIOSA stores the resulting access and refresh tokens, refreshes them automatically, and exposes the current valid access token to the sandbox as a placeholder env var.

**Resolver scope walk**
The ordered lookup MIOSA performs when a sandbox makes an outbound request and the proxy needs to match a placeholder to a real credential. The proxy checks scopes in this priority order: (1) direct sandbox binding, (2) user-scoped secret, (3) external_user-scoped secret, (4) external_workspace-scoped secret, (5) MIOSA workspace secret, (6) tenant-wide secret. First match wins. If nothing matches, the placeholder passes through unchanged and the upstream API call fails (the intended safe behavior).

## Real-world example  -  OpenAI customer-support agent in 5 minutes

This is the complete setup for an AI agent that uses OpenAI safely. Run these five commands and you're done.

**Python**

```python
import os
from miosa import Miosa

client = Miosa(api_key=os.environ["MIOSA_API_KEY"])

# 1. Create sandbox
sandbox = client.sandboxes.create(template_id="python-ds")

# 2. Store the OpenAI key  -  sandbox never sees the real value
sandbox.secrets.set(
    name="openai_key",
    value=os.environ["MY_OPENAI_KEY"],
    expose_as_env="OPENAI_API_KEY",
)

# 3. Lock down to only api.openai.com
sandbox.network.allow("api.openai.com")
sandbox.network.lockdown()

# 4. Run the agent  -  uses $OPENAI_API_KEY exactly like normal
result = sandbox.exec("""
python3 -c "
import os, requests
resp = requests.post(
    'https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions',
    headers={'Authorization': f'Bearer {os.environ[\"OPENAI_API_KEY\"]}'},
    json={'model': 'gpt-4o-mini', 'messages': [{'role': 'user', 'content': 'Hello!'}]}
)
print(resp.json()['choices'][0]['message']['content'])
"
""")
print(result.stdout)

# 5. Check the audit trail
events = sandbox.audit.list(since="5m")
for e in events:
    print(e.host, e.action, e.status_code)
```

## Troubleshooting

**My sandbox's env var contains a placeholder but the API returns 401.**
The proxy couldn't match the placeholder in the outbound request header. Confirm the SDK puts the token in `Authorization: Bearer ...`. See [troubleshooting #1](/docs/security/troubleshooting#1-secret-value-is-not-being-swapped-outbound-request-uses-the-raw-placeholder).

**I enabled lockdown and nothing works.**
Call `sandbox.network.pending()` to see the blocked hosts, then allow them. Or revert with `sandbox.network.observe()` while you diagnose.

**I can't see any audit rows.**
The audit log records outbound calls only. If the sandbox hasn't made any outbound requests, the log is empty. Trigger a call and re-query.

**I see "Reconnect needed" on a GitHub secret.**
The OAuth token was revoked by the user or expired. Call `sandbox.secrets.reauthorize(provider="github")` to re-run the OAuth dance. See [Connect Accounts troubleshooting](/docs/security/troubleshooting#4-github-oauth-refresh-failing--sandbox-gets-401-on-apigithubcom).

For the full list of issues and fixes, see the [Security troubleshooting hub](/docs/security/troubleshooting).
